abstract: Deploying recent natural language processing innovations to low-resource settings allows for state-of-the-art research findings and applications to be accessed across cultural and linguistic borders. One low-resource setting of increasing interest is _codeswitching_ , the phenomenon of combining, swapping, or alternating the use of two or more languages in continuous dialogue. In this paper, we introduce a large dataset (20k+ instances) to facilitate investigation of Tagalog-English code-switching, which has become a popular mode of discourse in Philippine culture. Tagalog is an Austronesian language and former official language of the Philippines spoken by over 23 million people worldwide, but it and Tagalog-English are under-represented in NLP research and practice. We describe our methods for data collection, as well as our labeling procedures. We analyze our resulting dataset, and finally conclude by providing results from a proof-of-concept regression task to establish dataset validity, achieving a strong performance benchmark (R<sup>2</sup> =0.797–0.909; RMSE=0.068–0.057).

bibliographic.title: TweetTaglish: A Dataset for Investigating Tagalog-English Code-Switching
bibliographic.venue: Proceedings of the 13th Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (LREC 2022)

content.problem: Tagalog and Tagalog-English code-switched text are under-represented in NLP because Tagalog data is scarce and standard NLP techniques perform poorly on mixed-language, word-level language identification tasks.
content.proposed_solution: The authors built TweetTaglish, a publicly released dataset of 21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched tweets collected via Tagalog keyword searches on Twitter and labeled with English, Tagalog, and Other word percentages using a dictionary-based word-level language identification method, and validated it with proof-of-concept regression experiments.
content.algorithm_or_model: Dictionary-based word-level language identification (Algorithm 1) with regression benchmarking models
dataset_testbed: TweetTaglish (21,150 Tagalog-English code-switched tweets collected from Twitter)

content.claim: Benchmarking experiments on TweetTaglish show the dataset is valid for machine learning, with a multilayer perceptron strongly outperforming a mean baseline at predicting tweet-level English, Tagalog, and Other language distributions (R2 of 0.797 to 0.909).
author_stated_limitations: The keyword search strategy can inadvertently include text from other non-English languages that share similar phrases, such as Spanish cognates like para.

Agreement between the automatic labeling method and human annotation was much lower at the word level (kappa of 0.15), partly because Spanish cognates captured during scraping were classified as Tagalog rather than Other.
Investigation of more complex code-switching tasks remains out of scope of the present paper.

evidence.problem_quote: Despite Tagalog's cultural importance within the Philippines, many cornerstones of modern natural language processing (e.g., syntactic and dependency parsers) are unavailable or underdeveloped for this widely spoken language (Aquino and de Leon, 2020). Tagalog data remains scarce (Manguilimotan and Matsumoto, 2011; Samson, 2018), and the language's typological differences from higher-resourced Austronesian languages such as Indonesian (Greenhill et al., 2009; Reid, 2018) hinder its further computational exploration.
evidence.proposed_solution_quote: This study contributes to this growing body of research by building TweetTaglish, a Tagalog-English code-switching dataset. The dataset is constructed from social media data, using Twitter as a resource.
evidence.claim_quote: As shown, we achieve our highest-performing results with MLP, with R2 values ranging from 0.797 (Other) to 0.909 (English) and RMSE ranging from 0.068 (Other and Tagalog) to 0.057 (English). The results clearly demonstrate validity of the dataset for machine learning models, as demonstrated by the observation that all models strongly outperformed the baseline Mean condition, setting the stage for future deeper exploration of Taglish code-switching.
author_stated_limitation_quotes: One minor observation was that our current keyword search strategy allowed for the inclusion of text from some other non-English languages with similar phrases (e.g., Spanish, due to cognates such as para).

Agreement was lower at the word level (κ = 0.15), owing in part to Spanish cognates such as para that were captured when scraping and subsequently classified by our algorithm as Tagalog rather than Other.

Although investigation of more complex CS tasks remains out of scope of the present paper, these experiments establish dataset learnability and provide initiative for follow-up work pursuing other CS tasks.
